title: What's this, and whose is it?
goal: Point to things by distance, ask what they're called in Korean, say who owns something, and — most important of all — start telling the particles 은/는 and 이/가 apart.
bekal: tell 이거, 그거 and 저거 apart by who the thing is close to
use 이, 그, 저 before a noun
show possession with 의 and drop it the way Koreans do
notice when a sentence uses 이/가 rather than 은/는

dialogs.title: 대화 — Things left behind in the classroom
dialogs.intro: After class, Ani finds a few things on the desk. Notice how the pointing words change according to who is closer to the object, not simply whether it's near or far.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: That's a dictionary. A Korean dictionary.
lines.literal: that — as-for — dictionary — is. Korea-language — dictionary — is.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: That over there is a clock. The classroom clock.
lines.literal: that-over-there — as-for — clock — is. classroom — clock — is.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.literal: this — book — as-for — who — thing — is?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.literal: that — as-for — my — thing — is. thank-you.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Is this bag yours too, Minjun?
lines.literal: this — bag — also — Minjun — Mr. — thing — is?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: No, that's not my bag. It's Suji's.
lines.literal: no, my — bag — subject — not-is. Suji — Ms. — thing — is.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: My friend. That person over there is Suji.
lines.literal: my — friend — is. that-over-there — person — subject — Suji — Ms. — is.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh, really? I'd like to be friends too.
lines.literal: ah, so — is? I — also — friend — subject — become — want.

notes: **Distance is measured from two people, not one.** 이거 = near the **speaker**. 그거 = near the **listener**. 저거 = far from **both**. That's why Ani asks with 이거 (the thing in her hand) and Minjun answers with 그거 (it's far from him). Two different words for the same object. English "this/that" only has two steps, so learners often take 그거 to mean "that, a bit far"; it really means "the one by you".

**이거/그거/저거 are shortened spoken forms.** The full forms are 이것/그것/저것. In conversation they're almost always shortened; formal writing and exams use the long forms. With a particle attached there are two options: 이거는 (casual speech) or 이것은 (writing). This module uses the spoken forms.

**이/그/저 without 거 go before a noun.** 이 책 = this book, 그 가방 = that bag, 저 사람 = that person over there. ⚠️ Don't write 이거 책 — that means "this, a book" as two separate things. If there's a noun, just use 이.

**거 in 제 거 means "thing belonging to".** The full form is 것. 제 거 = mine, 민준 씨 거 = Minjun's, 누구 거 = whose. The noun can be dropped when it's obvious: 그거는 제 거예요 = "that's mine", with no need to repeat "book".

**The possessive particle 의 is almost always dropped.** 제 친구의 가방 is grammatically correct, but Koreans say 제 친구 가방. Two nouns side by side are already understood as possession. Save 의 for formal writing; in speech, drop it. Also note that 의 here is pronounced *e*, not *ui*.
**도 replaces a particle; it doesn't stack on top of one.** 이 가방**은** → 이 가방**도** (this bag too). ⚠️ Don't write 이 가방은도. The same rule applies to 이/가 and 을/를: 제가 → 저도, 책을 → 책도.

**고맙습니다 and 감사합니다 both mean "thank you".** 감사합니다 comes from Chinese and sounds a little more formal; 고맙습니다 is native Korean and sounds a little warmer. Both are safe with anyone. The everyday form is 고마워요.
**저 meaning "I" and 저 meaning "over there" are two words that happen to look the same.** Context tells them apart, and in practice it's never confusing: 저 사람 almost can't mean "my person".

grammars.title: 은/는 vs 이/가 — the difference that matters most
body: This is the most important lesson in the whole module, and you won't finish it today. What you should take from this unit isn't mastery but **the awareness that the two are not the same thing**.
English has just one "subject"; Korean splits it into two different roles: what is being **talked about** (the topic, 은/는) and who **does something or is singled out** (the subject, 이/가).

head: After a vowel
After a consonant
What it does
rows: points out the doer or the one chosen

after: **First rule of thumb you can use right away: questions with 누구, 뭐, 어느 take 이/가, not 은/는.** 수지 씨**가** 누구예요? is right; 수지 씨는 누구예요? sounds as if you're comparing Suji with someone else.

**Second rule of thumb: 은/는 always carries a hint of contrast, even when it isn't said.** When Minjun says 그거는 제 거예요, it implies "that one is mine (the others, not necessarily)". That nuance is lost if you use 이/가.
**Third rule of thumb: self-introductions almost always use 은/는.** 저**는** 아니예요. You're setting yourself up as the topic of conversation, not picking yourself out of a crowd.
⚠️ Don't try to memorize the full rules now. Koreans themselves can't explain them. What works is noticing which one is used in each dialogue in this module, and copying it.

grammars.title: Basic question words
body: The seven question words below are enough to get by in everyday conversation. Each one goes **where the answer will go**, not moved to the front of the sentence as in English.
after: Look at 이거 뭐예요? — the question word sits exactly where the noun will appear in the answer: 이거 사전이에요. The word order doesn't change at all between question and answer.
누구 becomes **누가** when it's the subject: 누**가** 왔어요? (who came?), not 누구가. It's the only question word that changes form, and it comes up a lot.

blocks.text: The objects you'll point at most often in class, in your room and in your bag. Practice by pointing at real things around you while saying 이거 …이에요.

blocks.title: 휴대폰 and its relatives
items: A cell phone has three names, all in use: **휴대폰** (the most neutral), **핸드폰** (from *hand phone*, very common in speech), and just **폰** among young people.

Korean is full of English loanwords with their sounds reshaped to fit hangeul: 컴퓨터 (*computer*), 펜 (*pen*), 커피 (*coffee*), 버스 (*bus*), 택시 (*taxi*). Guessing often works — but don't get overconfident: 아르바이트 (part-time job) comes from German, and 원피스 means a dress, not a swimsuit.
That person over there is my friend.

exercises.prompt: Fill in 이거, 그거 or 저거.
items: The thing is in your hand, and you ask: ____ 뭐예요?
The thing is in the other person's hand: ____ 뭐예요?
The thing is at the far end of the room, away from both of you: ____ 뭐예요?
The other person is holding a book; you ask whose it is: ____ 누구 거예요?
You're holding a pen and say it's yours: ____ 제 거예요.

exercises.prompt: Fill in 은, 는, 이 or 가.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: 이거 뭐예요? — 그거는 사전이에요. — 이 책은 누구 거예요? — 그거는 제 거예요. — 그 가방은 제 가방이 아니에요. — 저 사람이 제 친구예요.
